min_other_p <- with(a1_cfa$item_coverage_65, min(p_present_weighted[!item %in% c("vdexf7z", "vdwdimmz", "any_item")]))

  if (abs(a - b) < tol) "about the same as" else if (a > b) "higher than" else "lower than"
}

## Purpose and overview

The Manly et al. (2022) algorithm classifies participants as having normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia from 5 cognitive performance domain scores estimated from an hour-long neuropsychological battery, together with an informant interview on cognitive and functional change (Langa et al., 2020). None of that data is available in the core interview. The HRS core interview (Crimmins et al., 2011; Ofstedal et al., 2005), has a brief battery of scored cognitive items (`r length(a1_cfa$items)` used here), 1 self-rated memory item, and an informant questionnaire that is only administered when a proxy answers for the respondent and no cognitive performance data is available. These cognitive measures are too few to score separate domains defined in HCAP, and the lack of informant reports on the daily function of a respondent who answers for themselves generates an important additional difference in available information.

To address these differences, we constructed an adaptation we call the "core algorithm", that follows the logic of the Manly-Jones algorithm with core measures and is calibrated to the Manly-Jones classifications of the same people at HCAP Wave 1 (2016). The core algorithm has 4 steps (Figure A1):

\(1\) a single cognitive factor score is estimated from the core items;

\(2\) the factor score is normed against the HRS-HCAP robust normative sample and expressed as a demographically adjusted T score;

\(3\) decision rules combine the T score, divided into 3 bands by 2 cut points, with self-rated memory change, or use the informant questionnaire when no cognitive tests were completed; and

\(4\) the 2 T-score cut points are set so that the weighted class shares produced by the Step 3 rules match those of the Manly-Jones algorithm at HCAP Wave 1 (2016).

Every parameter (item parameters, norms, and cut points) was estimated once using core data in the HRS-HCAP Wave 1 sample, and then held fixed and used for the classification of participants in the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 core interviews. A change in a participant's classification across waves will reflect changes in that participant's responses and/or age, but the scoring model does not change. The same item thresholds, norms, and cut points convert a 2022 response pattern exactly as they would convert the same pattern observed in 2016.

Self-rated concerns is a rating of memory worse than 2 years ago, and the \"yes\" arm includes don't know, refused, and not ascertained."

## Data

The analytic sample is the `r a1_n(a1_alg$hcap_n)` HRS-HCAP Wave 1 (2016) participants, followed in the HRS core interviews of 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022. The core algorithm uses 4 kinds of core data:

\(1\) the `r length(a1_cfa$items)` cognitive items in Table A1;

\(2\) self-rated memory compared with 2 years ago (HRS item D102: better, about the same, or worse);

\(3\) the 16-item informant questionnaire (IQCODE; Jorm, 1994), scored as the mean item rating from 1 (much improved) to 5 (much worse) and collected in proxy interviews; and

\(4\) age, sex, race and ethnicity (non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic), and years of schooling.

The calibration target for the core algorithm is the Manly-Jones classification algorithm as obtained in the HRS-HCAP Wave 1 sample. The Langa-Weir classification from the 2016 core interview (Crimmins et al., 2011) is used as a comparator used in the manuscript's sensitivity analysis, and we report its agreement with the Manly-Jones algorithm alongside that of the core algorithm.

## Approach: Step 1. A single cognitive score from the core battery

The core data can be used to generate a unidimensional composite of cognitive performance. We begin this with a single-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model. This model uses ordinal and binary items entered through probit thresholds, and the 3 continuous scores (animal naming, delayed word recall, and number series) were rescaled to the 0-1 range (continuous), all modeled as caused by a single general latent variable. The model was fit to HRS 2016 respondents aged 65 and older (N = `r a1_n(a1_cfa$n_obs)`) with the complex sample design and the HRS-HCAP Wave 1 weights. The use of HRS-HCAP Wave 1 weights means that those respondents not in the HRS-HCAP sample are included in the analysis with a weight of 0, so the estimates describe the population that HRS-HCAP represents (`r a1_n(a1_cfa$n_positive_weight_any_item)` HRS-HCAP participants with at least 1 HRS core item response). We first evaluate model fit in the pairwise complete sample with the weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted (WLSMV) estimator fit using Mplus software (version 9, Muthén & Muthén, Los Angeles, CA). Then, item parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR) and a probit link, which uses every available item response regardless of item missingness. The WLSMV approach is consistent with the missing completely at random assumption, whereas the MLR approach is consistent with the less restrictive missing at random assumption. In subsequent factor score estimation runs, all parameters were fixed at the HCAP Wave 1 maximum likelihood estimates. Expected a posteriori (EAP) factor scores (Bock & Mislevy, 1982) were estimated from the fixed model for every core person-wave from 2016 to 2022 with at least 1 item response (`r a1_n(a1_cfa$n_person_waves_scored)` person-waves, all ages). As with our analysis of the HCAP battery, immediate word recall was not included in the model because it adds little information beyond delayed recall in the HCAP Wave 1 sample (Jones et al., 2024).

## Results: Step 1. A single cognitive score from the core battery

The single-factor model fit well (RMSEA = `r a1_dec(fit$RMSEA_Estimate, 3)`, 90% CI `r a1_dec(fit$RMSEA_90CI_LB, 3)` to `r a1_dec(fit$RMSEA_90CI_UB, 3)`; CFI = `r a1_dec(fit$CFI, 3)`; TLI = `r a1_dec(fit$TLI, 3)`; SRMR = `r a1_dec(fit$SRMR, 3)`)^[RMSEA, root mean square error of approximation, estimates model misfit per degree of freedom in the population and does not compare the model with a baseline model. Lower values indicate better fit; values below 0.05 indicate close fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Steiger, 1990). CFI, comparative fit index, and TLI, Tucker-Lewis index, compare the fitted model with a baseline model in which the items are uncorrelated. Higher values indicate better fit; values of 0.95 or above indicate satisfactory fit (Bentler, 1990; Hu & Bentler, 1999; Tucker & Lewis, 1973). The TLI adds a penalty for model complexity. SRMR, standardized root mean square residual, is the average difference between the observed and model-implied correlations. Lower values indicate better fit; values of 0.08 or below indicate satisfactory fit (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2018; Hu & Bentler, 1999).] by the conventional guides. Standardized loadings in the MLR model ranged from `r a1_dec(a1_loading_range[1])` to `r a1_dec(a1_loading_range[2])` (Table A1), and that range indicates that no single item dominates the factor. Table A1 provides loadings from the MLR and WLSMV models. Loadings from the two estimators were similar for most items. The lower WLSMV loading for number series, the item with the most missing data (`r a1_pct(1 - a1_cov[["vdexf7z"]], 0)`% of HRS-HCAP participants with any core item response, against at most `r a1_pct(1 - min(a1_cov[names(a1_cov) != "vdexf7z"]), 0)`% for any other item), likely reflects how each estimator handles missing data. The higher WLSMV loading for object naming cannot be explained by missing data, which was nearly complete for that item. Instead, the difference may be related to the item's skewed response distribution (`r a1_pct(a1_cfa$top_share[["vdlfl2"]], 0)`% of HRS-HCAP participants named both objects correctly, weighted).

## Approach: Step 2. Demographic norms

The Manly-Jones algorithm defines impairment as performance more than 1.5 standard deviations below the level expected for a person's age, sex, race, ethnicity, and education in a robust normative sample (Manly et al., 2022). Although we use different thresholds to define impairment (discussed below), we norm the single general cognitive domain score the same way we normed domain scores in Manly et al. (2022).

The HCAP 2016 robust normative sample (n = `r a1_n(a1_norm$n_norm)`) is used to define "expected" cognitive performance levels. First, factor scores in the normative sample were converted to normal scores with the Blom (1958) rank transformation. Because this transformation is sample dependent, we derive a linking equation between Blom transformed scores and estimated factor scores using linear regression with a restricted cubic spline for the factor score (knots at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles; Harrell, 2015). The resulting regression model can be used to convert any factor score, including scores from people outside the normative sample and from later waves, to the normalized metric.

Second, the normalized score was regressed, with survey weights, on age (restricted cubic spline with knots at `r paste(a1_norm$age_knots, collapse = ", ")` years, centered at 70), sex, non-Hispanic Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, and years of schooling (centered at 12), together with their 2-way interactions (`r a1_norm$n_terms` terms). This demographic equation is used to estimate the expected score according to demographic characteristics.

Third, the sociodemographically adjusted cognitive performance score (T score) was computed as 50 + 10 × (observed − expected) / SEE, where SEE, the standard error of the estimate from the demographic regression in the normative sample, is the standard deviation of the normalized score multiplied by √(1 − R^2^). A T score of 40 therefore means performance 1 SEE below the level expected for a person of the same age, sex, race, ethnicity, and education. The same SEE is used regardless of demographic group, so a given T score marks the same distance below expectation for every participant.

## Results: Step 2. Demographic norms

The demographic equation explained `r a1_pct(a1_norm$r2, 0)`% of the variance in the normalized score in the normative sample. The standard deviation of the normalized score was `r a1_dec(a1_norm$pblom_sd, 3)`, and therefore the SEE was `r a1_dec(a1_norm$resid_sd, 3)` normalized-score units. In HRS-HCAP Wave 1, the unweighted mean (SD) T score was `r tf_mean("HCAP, normative sample")` (`r tf_sd("HCAP, normative sample")`) in the normative sample^[Manly et al. (2022) used the unweighted normative sample in this scale calibration step. An alternative would have been to use the sampling weights in the normative reference subpopulation group to set the mean (50) and standard deviation (10) on the rescaled cognitive performance measure. We use the convention established in Manly et al. (2022).] and `r tf_mean("HCAP, excluded from norms")` (`r tf_sd("HCAP, excluded from norms")`) among participants excluded from it.

## Step 3. Classification rules

In the Manly-Jones algorithm, dementia requires at least 2 impaired domains and an informant report of functional impairment, and MCI requires at least 1 impaired domain with informant-reported concern or self-reported memory worsening (Manly et al., 2022).

The core interview has no informant report for respondents who participated in the cognitive assessment. We replaced each element of the Manly-Jones rules with its closest core counterpart (Figure A1). We define every element of the rules here, before the cut points are set in Step 4, because the class shares that the cut points must match depend on all of them. The 2 T-score cut points (set in Step 4) stand in for the count of the number of domains impaired: T below the severe cut point (τ~1~) corresponds to impairment in 2 or more domains, and T between the severe and moderate cut points (τ~1~, τ~2~) corresponds to impairment in 1 domain. Self-rated memory worsening used in the Manly-Jones algorithm is a core item, and is used in place of informant report of cognitive functional impairment at both levels. Participants without core cognitive tests (mostly proxy interviews) were classified from the IQCODE with the Manly-Jones informant thresholds (`r a1_iq(a1_jorm_severe)` or higher for dementia; above `r a1_iq(a1_jorm_mild)` for MCI). Missing self-rated memory was singly imputed by chained equations (van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011)`r if (isTRUE(a1_alg$hcap_d102_imputed == 0)) "; no Wave 1 participant with a T score was missing self-rated memory" else paste0("; ", a1_n(a1_alg$hcap_d102_imputed), " Wave 1 participants with a T score")`, and "don't know," refused, and not ascertained responses (`r a1_n(a1_alg$hcap_d102_dk_rf_na)` participants) were counted as "worse", which assigns these participants to the more impaired class.

The core interview asks every self-respondent about limitations in activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), and these self-reports could stand in for the informant report of functional impairment that separates dementia from MCI in the Manly-Jones algorithm. We did not use them, for 2 reasons that do not depend on the cut points. First, few participants report any limitation, even among those the Manly-Jones algorithm classifies as having dementia. Among HRS-HCAP Wave 1 participants with a core T score and dementia by the Manly-Jones algorithm, `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_mj("Dementia"))`% (weighted) reported no ADL or IADL limitation, so no threshold on the limitation count can identify them. Second, the core items do not say why a limitation is present. Limitations from physical illness are common at these ages, and a rule that counts them would move participants with low T scores into the dementia class on the strength of a physical disability. The second criterion at both levels is therefore self-rated memory, an item the Manly-Jones algorithm already includes. The Endnote gives the full evidence and compares the rules at the cut points set in Step 4.

## Approach: Step 4. Cut points by prevalence matching

No point on a single T score corresponds by construction to 2 or more domains more than 1.5 standard deviations below expectation. With 5 domains, there are 10 different ways to satisfy exactly 2 domains impaired, and each would be associated with a different cut score on the single domain. No rule fixes in advance where on the T scale the cut points belong.

We therefore empirically identified 2 T-score (T representing the single domain cognitive performance measure, adjusted for sociodemographics and rescaled to a T distribution (M 50 SD 10) in the unweighted normative reference group) cut points: a severe cut point (τ~1~) and a moderate cut point (τ~2~). We set them by prevalence matching: with every other element of the rules fixed as described in Step 3, the cut points were chosen so that the weighted Normal, MCI, and dementia shares (*shares* meaning the weighted proportion in each classification) of the core algorithm approximate those of the Manly-Jones algorithm in HRS-HCAP Wave 1 (N = `r a1_n(a1_cal$n_sample)`). To check the choice, we evaluated every pair of cut points on a grid (severe cut point `r min(a1_cal$grid$cut_severe)` to `r max(a1_cal$grid$cut_severe)`, moderate cut point `r min(a1_cal$grid$cut_moderate)` to `r max(a1_cal$grid$cut_moderate)`, in steps of `r a1_cal$grid_step`) and located the pair that minimized the sum of squared differences between the 3 core and Manly-Jones shares, with ties broken by the higher weighted kappa. Among the 2 cut points, the dementia share depends only on τ~1~, and the MCI share depends on both. Each share also depends on the fixed parts of the rules: the self-rated memory item and the IQCODE thresholds. We matched shares, rather than maximizing agreement, because incidence and prevalence estimates depend on class shares; matching keeps population estimates from core data comparable to estimates from HRS-HCAP data. Matching shares does not guarantee that the same people are classified alike, and we report agreement separately below.

## Results: Step 4. Cut points by prevalence matching

The cut points were T < `r a1_cut(a1_used$cut_severe)` (severe) and T < `r a1_cut(a1_used$cut_moderate)` (moderate). With these cut points the weighted shares were `r a1_pct(a1_used$share_normal)`% normal, `r a1_pct(a1_used$share_mci)`% MCI, and `r a1_pct(a1_used$share_dementia)`% dementia, close to the `r a1_pct(a1_target[["1"]])`%, `r a1_pct(a1_target[["2"]])`%, and `r a1_pct(a1_target[["3"]])`% for the Manly-Jones algorithm estimated with EAP factor scores (Table A2). On the grid, the pair with the closest shares was T < `r a1_cut(a1_opt$cut_severe)` and T < `r a1_cut(a1_opt$cut_moderate)` (`r a1_pct(a1_opt$share_normal)`%, `r a1_pct(a1_opt$share_mci)`%, and `r a1_pct(a1_opt$share_dementia)`%); the cut points we used ranked `r a1_gpos$rank` of `r a1_n(a1_gpos$n_pairs)` pairs, and their largest difference from a Manly-Jones share was `r a1_dec(100 * a1_gpos$max_abs_share_diff_algorithm, 1)` percentage points, against `r a1_dec(100 * a1_gpos$max_abs_share_diff_calibrated, 1)` for the closest pair. The 3-class kappa was `r a1_dec(a1_used$kappa_3class)` with the cut points we used and `r a1_dec(a1_opt$kappa_3class)` with the closest pair; the dementia kappa was `r a1_dec(a1_used$kappa_binary)` and `r a1_dec(a1_opt$kappa_binary)`. `r if (a1_opt$kappa_3class <= a1_used$kappa_3class) "Because the closest pair moved the shares only slightly and did not improve agreement, we kept the cut points we used." else "We kept the cut points we used because the closest pair moved the shares only slightly."` The grid search also located the pair with the highest 3-class kappa (`r a1_dec(a1_maxk$kappa_3class)`, at T < `r a1_cut(a1_maxk$cut_severe)` and T < `r a1_cut(a1_maxk$cut_moderate)`), which gave `r a1_pct(a1_maxk$share_mci)`% MCI and `r a1_pct(a1_maxk$share_dementia)`% dementia; we did not use it because it does not reproduce the class shares. Figure A2 shows the distribution of T scores with the cut points, and Table A3 gives the rules with these cut points and the number of participants classified by each rule. The cut points were chosen and evaluated in the same sample, so the agreement statistics in Tables A2 and A4 are optimistic relative to what might be expected if both procedures were applied independently in a new cohort.

## Agreement with the Manly-Jones algorithm in HRS-HCAP Wave 1

We next examine the agreement of the core algorithm with the Manly-Jones classification and compare it with the agreement of the Langa-Weir classification, a widely used classification of cognitive status from HRS core data (Crimmins et al., 2011). For self-respondents, Langa-Weir sums immediate and delayed word recall (0 to 20), serial 7 subtraction (0 to 5), and backward counting (0 to 2) into a 27-point score, and classifies scores of 0 to 6 as dementia, 7 to 11 as cognitive impairment without dementia (CIND), and 12 to 27 as normal. For proxy interviews, it combines the proxy's report of the respondent's memory, limitations in instrumental activities of daily living, and the interviewer's assessment of cognitive impairment into an 11-point score, with 6 or more classified as dementia and 3 to 5 as CIND (cognitive impairment, not demented; Crimmins et al., 2011, pp. i164, i166). The Langa-Weir cut points were chosen so that the HRS distribution of cognitive states matches the distribution estimated in the Aging, Demographics, and Memory Study (ADAMS), the same prevalence-matching logic we used in Step 4, but the Langa-Weir score is not adjusted for demographic characteristics. We treat CIND as the counterpart of MCI.

Agreement of the core algorithm with the Manly-Jones algorithm for 3-class Normal/MCI/Dementia classification was `r cmp(ag$kappa_core, ag$kappa_lw)` the agreement of Langa-Weir; for dementia versus not, it was `r cmp(ag$kappa_core_bin, ag$kappa_lw_bin)` that of Langa-Weir (Table A4). The quadratic weighted kappa (Cohen, 1968) for the 3 classes was `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_core)` for the core algorithm and `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_lw)` for Langa-Weir; for dementia versus not, kappa was `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_core_bin)` and `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_lw_bin)`. Of the weighted population the Manly-Jones algorithm classified as having dementia, the core algorithm classified `r a1_pct(ag$capture_core, 0)`% as having dementia and Langa-Weir classified `r a1_pct(ag$capture_lw, 0)`%. Of those the core algorithm classified as having dementia, `r a1_pct(ag$ppv_core, 0)`% had dementia by the Manly-Jones algorithm (Langa-Weir: `r a1_pct(ag$ppv_lw, 0)`%). Agreement between the core algorithm and Langa-Weir was `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_core_lw)` (3 classes, weighted kappa) and `r a1_dec(ag$kappa_core_lw_bin)` (dementia, kappa). Table A5 gives the weighted cross-classifications. Each kappa compares 2 classifications that both contain error, so these values describe agreement and not accuracy.

## Application to the 2018, 2020, and 2022 core interviews

The fixed model, norms, and cut points were applied to every core interview of HRS-HCAP Wave 1 participants from 2016 to 2022 (Table A6). The number of classified person-waves fell from `r a1_n(w(2016, "classified"))` in 2016 to `r a1_n(w(2022, "classified"))` in 2022 as participants died or left the study, and the share classified from the IQCODE alone was `r a1_pct(w(2016, "iqcode") / w(2016, "classified"))`% in 2016 and `r a1_pct(w(2022, "iqcode") / w(2022, "classified"))`% in 2022.

```{r a1-table-6}
a1_table_waves
```

One wave departs from the others. Number series was not administered in the 2018 core interview (`r if (a1_numser_2018 == 0) "no 2018 respondent has a score" else paste(a1_n(a1_numser_2018), "2018 respondents have a score")`), so 2018 EAP scores are based on 7 items. With less information, an EAP score is pulled further toward the population mean (Bock & Mislevy, 1982), which raises the scores of low performers and may classify fewer participants as impaired in 2018 than the same performance would produce in other waves. We did not re-norm the 7-item score because the 7 items are in common with the 2016 core items and factor scores are estimated with fixed parameter estimates, therefore the factor score estimates are on the same scale (fixed parameter calibration).

Figure A3 and Table A7 compare EAP scores of core respondents aged 65 or older in 2018 (when number series was not administered) with those in 2016 and 2020 (combined, when number series was administered). The mean posterior standard deviation of the EAP score (the uncertainty in one participant's score given that participant's item responses, averaged over participants) was `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2018", "mean_psd"))` in 2018 and `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "mean_psd"))` in 2016 and 2020, and the standard deviation of the EAP scores (the spread of the score estimates across participants) was `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2018", "sd"))` and `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "sd"))`. Under the model, the variance of the EAP scores and the mean posterior variance sum to the factor variance of 1 (here `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2018", "total"))` in 2018 and `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "total"))` in 2016 and 2020), so `r if (a1_ss("2018", "mean_psd") > a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "mean_psd")) "the larger posterior variance in 2018 appears as a narrower distribution of EAP scores" else "the posterior variance in 2018 was not larger, and these data do not show added shrinkage"`. The lower quartile was `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2018", "q1"))` in 2018 and `r a1_dec(a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "q1"))` in 2016 and 2020. The effect on the spread of scores was small; the standard deviation of the 2018 EAP scores was about `r a1_pct(1 - a1_ss("2018", "sd") / a1_ss("2016 and 2020", "sd"), 0)`% smaller than in 2016 and 2020 (Table A7). A small shift for the population can still change the classification of individuals whose scores lie near a cut point. Because shrinkage moves low scores toward the mean, a participant whose T score would fall just below τ~1~ with number series may fall just above it without it, and be classified with MCI rather than dementia.

## Limitations

Limitations of our approach are worth mentioning.

First, the cut points were selected and evaluated in the same HRS-HCAP Wave 1 sample, so the agreement in Tables A2 and A4 is in-sample. The comparison of core-based and HRS-HCAP-based classifications among Wave 2 re-interviewees (eTables 7 and 8) is the out-of-sample check available in these data.

Second, self-rated memory replaces informant report, and `r if (fl$d2 / fl$b2 > 0.5) "most" else "many"` participants with low T scores did not report memory worsening; the core algorithm likely under-classifies dementia relative to the Manly-Jones algorithm, which is consistent with the lower core-based dementia incidence among re-interviewees in eTable 8.

Third, the 2018 scores rest on 7 items (above). The pattern of missingness for number series is difficult to discern from the data and the HRS concordance web tool.

Fourth, the norms do not account for interview mode, which varies across respondents and waves; a mode difference in test scores would shift T scores in the waves where the mode mix differs from 2016. Other potentially important considerations, such as language of administration, are not incorporated into the scoring and standardizing steps.

Fifth, the IQCODE in the core interview asks about change over 2 years, whereas the HRS-HCAP informant interview asks about change over 10 years, so the Manly-Jones IQCODE thresholds may not carry the same meaning in core proxy interviews.

Finally, both the core algorithm and the Manly-Jones algorithm rely on applying strict cut points to continuous cognitive, functional, and informant report measures. This practice of attempting to elicit qualitative clinical states from quantitative scales introduces well-documented classification instability, particularly for individuals whose scores fall near diagnostic thresholds (Streiner, 2002; Altman & Royston, 2006). Because continuous cognitive instruments inherently possess standard measurement error, small and clinically negligible fluctuations in test performance can shift an individual across an arbitrary boundary. As a result, observations that are quantitatively almost indistinguishable are operationalized as qualitatively distinct diagnostic categories, substantially inflating misclassification rates and generating spurious diagnostic changes across repeated assessments.

## Endnote. Why the core algorithm does not use functional limitations

Our original plan followed the Manly-Jones algorithm more closely. In the Manly-Jones algorithm, an informant report of functional impairment separates dementia from MCI (Manly et al., 2022), and the core interview asks every self-respondent about limitations in activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). We planned to use these self-reports in place of the informant report and to set their thresholds by prevalence matching within each level of cognitive impairment. We set the plan aside for 3 reasons, which we document here with the current data. The first and third reasons do not depend on the cut points and are summarized in Step 3. The comparison under the second reason uses the cut points set in Step 4, so it is a check made after the rules and cut points were fixed. Limitations were counted on the `r a1_fn$n_limit_items` ADL and IADL items asked in every core wave from 2016 to 2022 (Table A9 note), so that the count would mean the same thing in every wave.

First, few participants report any limitation, even among those the Manly-Jones algorithm classifies as having dementia. Among HRS-HCAP Wave 1 participants with a core T score, the weighted share reporting no ADL or IADL limitation was `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_mj("Dementia"))`% for those with dementia by the Manly-Jones algorithm, `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_mj("MCI"))`% for MCI, and `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_mj("Normal"))`% for normal cognition; below the severe T cut point, `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_band)`% reported none (Table A9). By definition, every participant the Manly-Jones algorithm classifies as having dementia has an informant report of functional impairment, yet `r a1_pct(a1_fn_none_mj("Dementia"))`% of them report no limitation in the core interview. The lowest possible threshold, 1 or more limitations, misses at least that share, and no threshold on the limitation count can do better.

Second, adding function `r a1_fn_effect_text`, and `r a1_fn_halves_text`. We applied 2 alternative rules, all at the core algorithm's cut points (T < `r a1_cut(a1_cut_severe)` and T < `r a1_cut(a1_cut_moderate)`), so that the rules differ only in the second criterion: function at the severe level and function or memory at the moderate level, the closest analog of the Manly-Jones rules; and function or memory at both levels (Table A10). In the full sample, the 3-class kappa was `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("memory", "kappa_3class"))` with the memory rule, `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("function", "kappa_3class"))` with the function rule, and `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("function_or_memory", "kappa_3class"))` with function or memory; the dementia kappa was `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("memory", "kappa_binary"))`, `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("function", "kappa_binary"))`, and `r a1_dec(a1_fn_var("function_or_memory", "kappa_binary"))`. Because the cut points are held fixed, the rules also produce different class shares (Table A10). To describe how much these differences vary across samples, we computed agreement in each of `r a1_fn$n_split` random halves of the sample (Table A11). Relative to the memory rule, the mean difference in 3-class kappa across halves was `r a1_shd_text("function", "kappa_3class")` for the function rule and `r a1_shd_text("function_or_memory", "kappa_3class")` for function or memory (2.5th to 97.5th percentile across halves), and the function rule had the higher kappa in `r a1_pct(a1_shd("function", "kappa_3class", "p_higher"), 0)`% of halves. For dementia, the mean differences were `r a1_shd_text("function", "kappa_binary")` and `r a1_shd_text("function_or_memory", "kappa_binary")`. `r a1_fn_conclusion_text`

Third, the core items do not say why a limitation is present. A participant who cannot bathe without help because of hip arthritis and a participant who cannot bathe without help because they no longer remember the steps give the same answer. Limitations from physical illness are common at the ages of HRS-HCAP participants, and a rule that counts any limitation would move some participants with low T scores into the dementia class on the strength of a physical disability. We judged that the gain in agreement was not large enough to justify letting limitations with probable physical causes enter the dementia classification. We kept the memory rule, which uses an item the Manly-Jones algorithm already includes. An earlier version of this analysis, with different cut points and an unweighted subsample, found the same floor: within each level of cognitive impairment, fewer participants reported any limitation than had functional impairment by the Manly-Jones algorithm, so no threshold on the limitation count could match the HRS-HCAP rates.
